title: GalaxEye Secures US Patent for Dual-Sensor Satellite Imaging in Boost for India's Space Ambitions
excerpt: The IIT Madras-founded startup becomes the first Indian company to win a US patent for satellite imaging technology, covering its OptoSAR system that combines optical and radar sensors on a single platform.
body:
• GalaxEye has secured a US patent for its OptoSAR imaging system, which synchronises optical and synthetic aperture radar sensors on a single satellite to capture aligned Earth observation data in any weather or lighting conditions.
  • The Bengaluru-based startup, founded by IIT Madras engineers, says it is the first Indian company to receive a US patent for satellite imaging technology.
  • GalaxEye plans to build a 30-satellite constellation over the next five years and recently acquired spacecraft engineering firm StarOps to strengthen its manufacturing capabilities.
  • The global commercial satellite imaging market is projected to grow from $6.55 billion in 2024 to $20.15 billion by 2033, according to SkyQuest Technology.

Indian space technology startup GalaxEye has secured a United States patent for the core technology behind its OptoSAR imaging system, marking a milestone for India's rapidly growing commercial space sector. The patent covers a system that synchronises optical and synthetic aperture radar sensors to capture precisely aligned images of the same location simultaneously — a capability that addresses one of the longstanding challenges in Earth observation.

The company said it is the first Indian startup to receive a US patent for satellite imaging technology. The same foundational technology has already been patented in India.

How OptoSAR Works

Satellite Earth observation has traditionally relied on two distinct sensing technologies. Optical sensors capture detailed visual and spectral images — useful for identifying vegetation, infrastructure and water bodies — but depend on clear skies and daylight. Synthetic aperture radar uses microwave signals to observe the ground, operating through cloud cover, darkness and adverse weather, but producing a different type of data.

https://x.com/PriyankKharge/status/2097589954121810391

Combining these two data types has historically required stitching together images taken at different times, angles or from different satellites, introducing temporal gaps and spatial misalignment that reduce accuracy.

GalaxEye's patented architecture mounts both sensor types on a single satellite and synchronises them at the system level, producing spatially and temporally matched data in a single pass. The result is what the company calls weather-agnostic imaging — reliable data regardless of cloud cover, time of day or atmospheric conditions.

"This is not just a patent for us. This is an invention — an invention that came out of India. We are building global-first technology truly in India — not importing it, not adapting it, but inventing it here."

— Suyash Singh, Co-founder and CEO, GalaxEye

Mission Drishti and Constellation Plans

The patent is closely tied to GalaxEye's Mission Drishti, launched on May 3, 2026. At roughly 190 kilograms, the satellite was described as India's largest privately built Earth observation satellite at the time of launch and the world's first OptoSAR imaging satellite, combining multispectral imaging and radar on a single platform.

The mission has allowed GalaxEye to validate its technology in orbit and understand system performance under actual operating conditions. The company plans to deploy two additional satellites over the next 24 months, followed by full-scale deployment of a 30-satellite constellation over five years.

Singh said the objective is not simply to reach a satellite count but to build persistent coverage. "Our vision is to build a constellation that gives us a much more persistent view of the Earth," he told The Hindu BusinessLine.

Growing Commercial Pipeline

GalaxEye, which has raised approximately $21 million in funding to date, is already commercially active across defence, agriculture and forestry. The company is evaluating global markets where persistent, all-weather observation is in demand, including insurance, maritime intelligence, infrastructure monitoring and disaster management.

In August, GalaxEye acquired Bengaluru-based spacecraft engineering company StarOps to strengthen its in-house manufacturing and satellite system capabilities. The acquisition is part of a broader effort to control more of the satellite value chain as the company scales toward constellation-level production.

The patent comes as the global commercial satellite imaging market enters a period of rapid growth. Research firm SkyQuest Technology valued the market at $6.55 billion in 2024 and projects it will more than triple to $20.15 billion by 2033, driven by rising demand for satellite-based intelligence across security, agriculture, insurance and disaster response.

India's Space Sector Momentum

GalaxEye's patent adds to a series of milestones for India's private space industry, which the government expects to grow into a $44 billion sector within the decade. The Indian Space Research Organisation has steadily opened the sector to private companies, and startups like GalaxEye, Skyroot Aerospace and Agnikul Cosmos are pushing India's presence in commercial space beyond government-led missions.

For Singh, the US patent carries significance beyond intellectual property protection. "The US patent validates the ability of Indian deep-tech companies to develop globally differentiated technology," he said, framing GalaxEye's achievement as a signal that India can compete at the frontier of space technology, not just adapt innovations developed elsewhere.
image_caption: GalaxEye's Mission Drishti satellite during launch preparations on May 3, 2026. The 190-kilogram spacecraft is India's largest privately built Earth observation satellite and the world's first to combine optical and radar sensors on a single platform.
nri_angle: GalaxEye's US patent win underscores the growing role of IIT-trained founders in building globally competitive deep-tech companies from India, a trend that resonates with the diaspora's pride in Indian innovation.
